edbDesc: (or superelasticity) An elastic (impermanent) response to relatively high stress caused by a phase transformation between the austenitic and martensitic phases of a crystal. Exhibited in Shape memory alloys. Superelastic alloys belong to the larger family of shape memory alloys. Unlike shape-memory alloys, no change in temperature is needed for the alloy to recover its initial shape.
title: Superelasticity
description: Certain alloys, above all nickel-titanium, can be bent or stretched far more than ordinary metal and spring right back, because the strain flips their crystals into another arrangement that flips back when let go. Arne Ölander first saw such rubbery behaviour in a gold-cadmium alloy in 1932; nickel-titanium ('Nitinol') came from the US Naval Ordnance Laboratory in 1962. It is used in eyeglass frames you can twist, orthodontic wires and artery stents.
effect: an alloy bent far out of shape springs fully back as its crystals change form and change back
strength: Nitinol springs back from about 8% stretch, roughly ten times more than spring steel.
pickWhy: Borderline: Judgment call: comes from the same crystal flip as shape memory alloys (another batch), so a merge is arguable; picked a separate card named Superelasticity (clearer than pseudoelasticity) since springing back is a different job from remembering a shape when heated. The 1932 Ölander date is from memory.
